images.caption: Figure 1:Scene and personal-memory examples.Each row shows a query image, user request, retrieved personal memory, and response snippets from PReMind-4B and comparison models. “Personalization-focused” and “Safety-focused” describe each comparator answer’s behavior, not trained specialists. Memory tags indicate memory type (TableS.4).

Figure 2:Scenario map.Every request includes an image. (a) A single visual scene and its memory store support requests requiring different evidence. (b) Requests are categorized by required evidence: personal fact (PF), safety knowledge (SK), both, or scene only (SO). CALL requests require memory retrieval, whereas DIRECT requests do not. Risk (safe vs. unsafe) varies independently.

header: 5PReMind: Jointly Learning Memory Use and Hazard Response

images.caption: Figure S.1:Training and test coverage.Hazard groups H2–H5 appear only in test; memory-dependent non-acute risks occur in both splits.
Figure S.2:Disjoint capture scenes.Unedited frames from training/validation scenes (top) and test scenes (bottom).
Figure S.3:Geometry-guided image compositing.Regions of interest (RoIs) derived from scene geometry constrain masked edits when inserting reference entities.

Figure S.5:Interdependency examples.Cases involving a running saw, falling kitchenware and bleeding show the scene, target and look-alike memories, and model responses. Ticks and crosses indicate reference-based verdicts on full answers, not harm labels. Memory tags denote memory types (TableS.4). Names and other personal details are assigned per request, so the same person may carry different names across examples.

Figure S.6:Two-turn memory interaction.The agent decides whether to call memory from the image and request, then answers with any retrieved context. Visible acute hazards require a response even when personal evidence is missing; a memory call alone does not warn the user.

Figure S.7:Personal-fact use and response detail.Verbatim responses; blue marks selected PReMind advice, red the SFT allergy mismatch in (a), and brown conditional wording in (b). (a) The memory quote is expanded for readability; the evaluated inputs and responses are verbatim. (b) Both pass under both judges and recommend the blue reliever. SFT also gives conditional choking/CPR advice; its presence alone does not establish harm.
Figure S.9:Human preference on acute-hazard requests.Results are grouped by baseline correctness under the automatic scorer; values are percentages of judgments.

Figure S.13:Memory-use and hazard-response failures.Verbatim responses from PReMind-4B and Opus 5.5. The first two PReMind answers omit personal adaptations in the reference; the third omits a reference action for the visible knife hazard. These omissions are scored separately from critical harm.
